lede: Before any mechanics question can be answered the forces have to be found and named. A force diagram is that list, drawn: one arrow for every push or pull on the body, each with a label. Get the picture right and the equations almost write themselves.
can: Name every force acting on a body and show it as a labelled arrow
Place weight, normal reaction, tension and friction correctly, on the flat and on a slope
Decide what belongs on a force diagram and what does not

md: Push a book across a table and four things act on it: the Earth pulls it down, the table pushes it up, your hand pushes it along, and the surface drags it back. A force diagram is a way of saying all four at once, in one picture.

text: 1. One arrow, one label, one force

alt: A crate of mass 6 kg on a rough horizontal floor. Four arrows leave the crate: R straight up, 60 N straight down, T up to the right along a rope at 26 degrees to the floor, and F to the left along the floor.

caption: Four forces on a crate: reaction, weight, tension and friction.

md:
Each force gets a straight arrow drawn from the body, pointing the way that force acts, and a label of its own. Nothing else belongs there: no speeds, no accelerations, no masses.

A label of $6$ kg would be a mass. The force the Earth causes is the weight, $60$ N, and that is what the arrow is for.

prompt: On the force diagram above, the arrow pointing straight down from the crate is labelled 60 N. Which force is it?
options: the normal reaction on the crate
explain: The Earth pulls the crate down with a force of $6 \times 10 = 60$ N. A mass would be in kilograms and is not a force at all.

text: 2. Weight is $mg$, and it points straight down

caption: Tilt the surface and the weight does not tilt with it.

md:
Weight is the pull of the Earth on the body, $W = mg$, and this paper takes $g = 10$ m/s². So a mass of $9$ kg has a weight of $90$ N.

The Earth pulls the same way whatever the surface is doing, so the weight arrow is vertical on the flat and still vertical on a slope. It is drawn from the centre of the body.

prompt: A box has a mass of 7 kg. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is its weight, in newtons?
explain: $W = mg = 7 \times 10 = 70$ N. The mass is in kilograms; the weight it causes is in newtons.

caption: On a slope the reaction $R$ is at right angles to the slope, not to the ground.

md:
A surface cannot pull. The part of its push that comes straight out of it is the normal reaction: on a floor that is vertically up, and on a slope it is at right angles to the slope.

One contact gives one normal reaction, so a body resting on a single surface never carries two.

title: Why the push is perpendicular
md: The surface pushes only because the body is trying to sink into it, and sinking in is a movement straight into the surface. So the push that stops it comes straight back out, at right angles. Anything acting along the surface is friction, which is a separate force with a separate label.

prompt: A box rests on a slope inclined at 24° to the horizontal. In which direction does the normal reaction on the box act?
options: at right angles to the slope
answer: at right angles to the slope
explain: Vertically upwards would be the reaction on a horizontal floor. Up the slope is the direction friction or a rope would take.

caption: The block slides down, so friction $F$ acts up the slope.

md:
Friction acts along the surface and against the sliding, so a block sliding down a slope has friction pointing up it. Turn the motion round and friction turns with it.

A string can only pull, so its tension acts along the string, away from the body. A rough surface gives friction; a smooth one gives none, so none is drawn.

title: Force diagrams
why: The same four forces put on several bodies in turn. Watch how each arrow is drawn from the body and labelled before any arithmetic starts.

prompt: A block slides down a rough slope. In which direction does the force due to friction on the block act?
explain: Friction opposes the sliding. The block slides down, so friction acts up the slope, along the surface.

md:
When two bodies are joined, each one gets its own complete set of forces. The block on the table has a reaction and friction; the hanging block has neither, because it touches nothing.

A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension all the way along, so both ends take the same label $T$. Two different strings take two different letters.

prompt: Two blocks are joined by a light string passing over a smooth pulley. The tension pulling one block is labelled T. What label should the tension pulling the other block carry?
explain: One string carries one tension, so the same letter is used at both ends. A second string would need a second letter.

alt: A two-column table. What belongs on a force diagram: the weight in newtons, one reaction per contact, the tension along each string, and friction on a rough surface. What does not belong: the mass in kilograms, a second reaction on one surface, the components of the weight, and the velocity or the acceleration.

md:
An invented force costs a mark as surely as a missing one. The commonest inventions are a second reaction on one surface, friction on a surface described as smooth, and a force drawn down a slope.

That last one matters: the pull down a slope is part of the weight, not a new force. Splitting the weight into components is working, and working belongs beside the diagram.

title: What the reports keep saying
md: Two marks for a diagram are among the cheapest in the paper, and about half the entry misses one of them: a reaction left off, friction pointing the wrong way, or a force that was never there.

prompt: A box rests on a rough slope. Which one of these should not be drawn as a force on the box?
options: the component of the weight down the slope
answer: the component of the weight down the slope
explain: That component is part of the weight, which is already on the diagram. Drawing it as well counts the same pull twice.

md:
Name the four forces that turn up on Unit 2 diagrams and draw each as a labelled arrow.
Place the weight vertically from the centre and the reaction at right angles to the surface.
Turn friction to face the sliding, and give one string one tension label.
Give each body of a connected pair its own complete set of forces.
Leave off masses, components and anything that is not a push or a pull.

The opening part of a mechanics question asks you to show every force on the body, on a diagram already printed for you, and it carries two marks: one for roughly half the forces, one for the rest. The first mark is for arrows pointing the right way with labels; the last is for having them all and nothing extra. Stuck? Work round the body: Earth, surface, string, sliding.
